Paratantram
Published by Lieutenant Colonel Sri Dhana Shamsher Jung Bahadur Rana.
Caṇḍī Kāryālaya, Prayāga-6. First Edition, Saṃvat 2016.
Homage to Śrī Lalitā Tripurasundarī.
The First Chapter:
In the Karavīraka cremation ground, which is filled with many supernatural powers (siddhis),
all the hosts of heroes were engaged in loud, boisterous laughter.
In the yoga of the great wheel that has been turned within the mandala of the thirty [gods], O Great Host, O Great Shaker, when the Ḍākinīs are invoked in battle! || 2 ||
The eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, Kṣetreśa, Bhairava, and the others, Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, and the Siddhas, are present in the assembly of the Mātṛcakra.
All the hosts beginning with Śrīnātha [are present] in the incarnation of Vīranātha;
by the grace of Siddhinātha, Kuleśvara is satisfied.
Having cast aside all ornaments, with a mind overflowing with joy and exaltation,
Kulasundarī questioned the Lord who was established in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya).
The illustrious Goddess said:
"By your grace, I have heard the knowledge proclaimed in all the scriptures,
including the eight Yāmalas and various kinds of Tantras."
The severing of the head in many ways, the great Manthāna-ṣaṭka,
and the ocean-water in the Mālātantra and the Vītkāra, O high-minded one.
(2) "Indeed, all twenty-four lakhs [of verses] have been heard by me as they were proclaimed;
yet now, O Lord, a doubt has arisen within me because of your very words."
She is that one supreme power, the non-dual Sovereign Goddess;
she is the one power, Mahāmāyā, who remains pervading the entire universe.
Neither beginning, middle, nor end— by which everything proceeds—
was that second [nature] spoken of by you in the *Kulamahārṇava-tantra*.
"This single [goddess], worshipped by the three worlds, sustains the entire universe.
O Lord, how is it that this very word of Brahmā is the sixfold tradition (ṣaḍāmnāya)? (11)
The goddesses seated upon the six thrones are declared to be the six leaders (ṣaṇṇāyikās);
yet how can she alone, who is indeed differentiated by the six traditions (āmnāyas), be the Supreme One? 12.
"O God, Lord of the World, tell me: are you undivided or divided?
How is it that the one supreme Śakti, the Supreme Goddess, has become manifold? (13)
O Goddess, the six leaders seated upon the six thrones are proclaimed;
if they are distinguished by the six Āmnāyas, what difference does it make other than by the distinction of their names? (14)
The goddess who was on the eastern lion-throne has taken refuge on the southern lion-throne;
she who was on the western lion-throne is the supreme one on the northern lion-throne.
She who is situated above the lion-throne and yet seated below the lion-throne,
established upon six lion-thrones, is celebrated as the Sixfold Tradition (Ṣaḍāmnāya).

How is it that the lion-throne is established as a conceptual designation for the deity of the tradition (āmnāyadevatā), whether in the Tantra or in the Yāmala consisting of twenty-four lakṣas? || 17 ||
In your scripture, she has indeed been indicated specifically through the six Āmnāyas;
is she one, supreme, and yet divided, or does she reside upon the six lion-thrones? (18)
How has the primordial power, which is indeed one and supreme, come to possess sixfold nature—that primordial, subtle Prakṛti which exists in differentiated forms? (19)
"She exists in every way as the primordial state in the form of Bindumālinī;
O Supreme Lord, resolve this great doubt of mine. (20)
O Omniscient Supreme Lord, at the time of emergence, the knot is very firm;
if there is but one supreme power, the primordial sovereign Prakṛti. (21)
For what purpose and for whose protection were the six Āmnāyas proclaimed?
They are for the sake of protecting the three worlds and for the preservation of the *samaya*.
O Supreme Lord, speak only for the sake of the practitioner’s prayer.
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O most beloved goddess; I shall tell you. I declare to you that which is more secret than the secret, divine, and otherwise untold.
Out of affection for you, I shall proclaim the secret of the Kaulika lineage;
having offered salutations with "Oṃ," I shall proclaim Viṣṇu-māyā, who consists of the entire universe. 24.
She is Nārāyaṇī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the primordial nature (Prakṛti) whose form is the universe;
she is the one supreme and lower power, the Prakṛti who deludes the entire world.
Because she deludes the universe, she is celebrated as Vaiṣṇavī;
because she sustains, they call her Dhātrī, and because she protects, she is the Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī).
Through the contemplation of her nature as the deluder of the three worlds, she is known as Prakṛti;
because she sustains the universe, she is celebrated as Vaiṣṇavī. (27)
Māyā, who bestows liberation as absolute isolation (kaivalya), is known as Nārāyaṇī;
even the Lord is under her control, like many birds on a string.
Without whom even the Supreme Lord is called a corpse;
without her, the Supreme Lord is not able to live at all. (29)
Even the Lord becomes powerless without the perception of Prakṛti;
just as fire, though present in wood, is not manifested until it is produced by friction.
Indeed, one who is fully possessed by Māyā becomes the agent of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
for just as a body devoid of the individual soul (jīva) is not able to move at all. || 31 ||
O Dear One, because he is devoid of activity like a corpse, he remains established in samādhi;
thus he is praised during the time of night as being free from māyā.
The Lord is indeed motionless like a corpse due to the gathering of the garland of points (bindu-mālinī);
having swallowed [all] through Māyā, he is designated as Śiva.
Through the union of Śiva and Śakti, this entire world comes into being;
that Māyā, in the form of consciousness, remains pervading the universe. (34)
I am the god Sadāśiva, and Prakṛti is called Viṣṇu;
O Goddess, from the union of these two, they are celebrated as Śiva and Śakti. (35)
She is the one who causes the wheel of saṃsāra to revolve for all beings;
but you, O Goddess, are the Māyā of Viṣṇu, whose very self is the world of Nārāyaṇa.
"O God, I know myself to be of the nature of bliss; O Sadāśiva, O Goddess, I thus set both gods Hari and Hara into motion. (37)
How do creation, maintenance, and dissolution occur in every kalpa? Behold with your divine eye that the universe consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti. 38.
Since the offspring are neither marked with the lotus, nor marked with the thunderbolt, nor marked with the wheel,
but rather marked with the male organ and the female organ, therefore the offspring belong to Maheśvara.
By her the Creator brings forth what is created; Hari protects it in eight ways;
Rudra withdraws it as the Destroyer; all the gods are his followers.
That one supreme Goddess stands pervading the universe;
through the twenty-four principles, she brings consciousness to the cosmic egg.
Assuming a body composed of earth, air, ether, water, and fire,
he creates the universe at his will in kalpa after kalpa.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva;
the body consists of the five elements and is composed of the five [categories]. || 43 ||
Having been unified, they thus exist in the form of the five elements;
the lifeless has come to the state of the five elements through the form of the living soul.
The union of the five elements is the great tradition (mahāmnāya) of the lion-throne;
she is the primordial, supreme Śakti, abiding in the void and the protectress of Kula. 45.
Pervading the entire universe, eternal, and having the nature of the Supreme Brahman;
she is the embodiment of all seeds through the twenty-four principles. || 46 ||
She who is the very nature of Brahman is directly divided by the distinction of female and male;
eternal and assuming the form of Lalitā, she sports in play. (47)
O Śivā, though formless, she assumes a form and maintains a male form;
sometimes, for sport, the Goddess plays by means of a form of māyā.
Sometimes by her own will she assumes the form of Hari, sometimes the form of Śiva;
indeed, Māyā assumes the form of Brahmā, while the Supreme (Parā) assumes the form of Will.
This goddess, both supreme and non-supreme, is primordial nature (prakṛti), the deluder of the universe;
she sets the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) in motion and, together with Samaya, acts for its protection.

For the sake of attaining the siddhi of the lineage of Śrīnātha, the Goddess has come to possess the nature of the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya); I shall now tell you in brief how she resides upon the six lion-thrones.
O Goddess, formerly in the secluded Ānandavana, which was devoid of animals, I, as Sadāśiva, took refuge in the meditation and concentration upon the six cakras. (52)
But you, having become a Kāpālinī, questioned me regarding the six lineages (ṣaḍanvaya):
first, that which is with the eastern face and with the form of Tatpuruṣa.
The Eastern [direction], however, spoke of the Supreme Śiva as Tatpuruṣa, who is the Great Being seated upon the lion-throne and who is the Heroine, the Power of Rudra.
Pūrṇeśvarī, the most formidable, is proclaimed in the Eastern Tradition (pūrvāmnāya);
I shall now describe her as the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśvarī) for the benefit of practitioners. 55.
But having established the mind in meditation (dhyāna), the Supreme Goddess should be meditated upon—She who resembles a sapphire in luster and who bears ten staff-like arms. (56)
In his lotus-like hands, he holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a beautiful trident, a skull-cup, a hand-drum, a rosary, and a spear. (57)
Holding a sugarcane bow and an arrow, with a sword in her hand, she is most beautiful;
she is seated there upon a great preta, established on a throne of the moon and sun.
She stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, has three eyes, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads;
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla have become her earrings.
She is adorned with an endless garland of necklaces and decorated with various types of neck-ornaments;
she has three large eyes and wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
This goddess Pūrṇeśvarī is fond of the sound of the "hā hā" cry;
she is renowned as Pūrṇeśvarī, possessed of ego and joined with the quality of rajas.
On the mountain at the seat (pīṭha) of Pūrṇālaya, in the cremation ground of Lakṣmīvana,
the eternal Nityā, who descends in many forms, was worshipped by Indra.
Renowned as the Pūrvāmnāya, she is worshipped by the ancient gods and sages;
she is the sovereign of all sciences and brings about a weight of great fortune.
She who assumes various forms, eternal, and the one who descends in many forms; Jayā, Jayantī, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Nārasiṃhikā. || 64 ||
Vyāghreśvarī, Karālā, Rājeśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Raktadantā, Viśālākṣī, Kāmeśī, and Caṇḍamālinī. || 65 ||
Vidyujjihvā, Ḍāmareśī, Nāṭeśī, Nṛtyanāyikā, Nandī, Mahākālī, Bhṛṅgiṇī, and Kulālikā. (66)
There, Navanāṭeśvarī is endowed with the four and five rasas;
she is the goddess of gods with many divisions, as are the eight Bhairavas and the Mātṛkās. (67)
She is renowned as Nāṭeśvarī, Bhairavī, and Cakrapālikā; [so too are] Kṣetrapāla, Vighneśa, Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, and the group of eight Mothers (Mātṛkāṣṭaka).
The Brahmāṇīs and others are worshipped there; the maiden Kumārī always grants desires.
O God, in ancient times, Bhairava was surrounded by the Mothers while dancing.
She named Nṛtyabhairavā is established in the eastern wheel;
the Gaṇeśas, Kṣetras, and Ḍākinīs, as well as the Gaṇas, are dependent upon Tatpuruṣa.
Having propitiated [the deity] on the left-hand path, and not through rites on the right,
they followed that [path] in many ways in Plakṣadvīpa and Kuśadvīpa.
Subjugation, attraction, and immobilization, as well as the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*—
having propitiated Marīci, he bestowed these upon Śakra.
Thus was this ancient tradition [established] by her while she sat upon the eastern lion-throne.
Thus ends the first chapter, concerning the lineage of the Eastern Tradition of Pūrṇeśī, in the glorious Parātantra. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter: Regarding the Dakṣiṇāmnāya, I shall speak of her who is of great heroism and exceedingly fierce, ordained by Aghorabhairava, the Mistress of Night, and free from all bonds.
The eternal Goddess Nirālambeśvarī is known as Aghora, whose head is that [of the deity];
the eternal Niśeśī, smeared with red, is seated upon a lion-throne.
Some call her Caitanyabhairavī, some Raktakālī;
some Sundarī Kālikā, and some Aghoreśvarī. (3)
I shall now describe the form of meditation for Bhairavī, who resides in the southern direction:
she is eternal, devoted to the partless, the mistress of night, and the refuge of those beyond the gunas.
In ancient times, O Goddess, the goddess Caitanyabhairavī was propitiated by Dharmarāja through his ritual sacrifice (kratu), as he acted as the bestower of the lineage transmission. || 5 ||
The Goddess, seated upon the four Vedas, established in the great *phetkāra*,
blazing in the midst of the funeral pyre, is the supreme bestower of skill in the right path.
Like a whirling firebrand, her garlands of skulls revolve;
she is emaciated, with sinews for her ornaments, her limbs wasted away, and reduced to mere bone and skin. (7)
Her waist was wrapped in a tiger skin, and she wore a human skin as an upper garment;
she resembled a thousand suns and possessed the brilliant luster of refined gold.
She has five faces and is exceedingly terrifying, endowed with fifteen eyes;
she has a slightly smiling face and a lolling tongue, with a deep navel and a slender waist. (9)
Seated upon a formidable throne, she dwells on a seat with the face of a wheel;
she is Raudrī, the dispeller of fear, the terrible one whose banner is marked by the crescent moon.
With half her hair disheveled and half bound, she is adorned by the king of serpents;
she possesses a headless torso and a turban, with the head of Brahmā as the crest-jewel upon her crown. || 11 ||
Adorned with a garland of freshly severed human heads and dripping with the blood of the world,
she is endowed with sixteen arms and wears an elephant’s skin and small bells.
A noose, a goad, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a severed head, and a small drum;
a sword, a shield, an arrow, a bow, a discus, a staff, and a water-pot.
With her hands displaying the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons, as well as the raised index finger,
she is joyful and now surrounded by powers (śaktis) who have attained success.
Terrifying the hosts of deities with the sound of the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*,
he stood above the Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva.
Mahādeva is in the form of a Śava, stationed upon the heart;
she is Niśeśī and Mahogrā, who is devoid of the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra). || 16 ||
There exists a distinction between the senior and the junior [forms] residing upon the southern lion-throne;
all its limb-deities are manifold and exceedingly powerful. (17)
Jaṃbhinī, Staṃbhinī, Nārāmohinī, Andhinī, Śivā, Mṛtyuñjayā, Carcikā, Siṃhī, and Dakṣiṇakālikā. || 18 ||
Pracaṇḍā, Ugracaṇḍā, Ugratārā, Kapālinī, Tvaritā, Chinnaśīrṣā, and Vagalā, the bestower of speech. (19)
Nīlā, Sarasvatī, Bhīmā, Trailokyada mareśvarī, Trailokyavijayā, Caṇḍī, Raktacāmuṇḍī, and Bhairavī. || 20 ||
The Goddess of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya) extends through various divisions;
she consists of the eight [forms] beginning with Brahmā, the eight Bhairavas, and likewise the eight Kṣetrapālas.
The hosts of Yoginīs [worship] Vaṭuka, Gaṇeśa, and the Lord of their own field;
she alone, though possessing diverse forms, is the Samayī for the sake of protection.
All the hosts of Aghora, surrounded by various attendants, filled the quarters of the sky with the great and fierce roar of their laughter. (23)
There, he was surrounded by many *vetālas* and throngs of *ḍākinīs*;
having assumed the playful behavior of a child, he was encircled by hosts of night-stalkers.
With staffs and nooses raised in their hands, they grant success to all practitioners;
in the islands of Śāka and Puṣkara, she reveals herself as non-different from the practitioner. 25.
Those who dwell in the crossroads, the thickets, the sacred seats, and the path of the Yoni-maṇḍala;
those devoted to the left-hand practice (vāmācāra) should indeed be worshipped, for they bestow the eight supernatural powers beginning with aṇimā.
I have proclaimed this as a sūtra, in accordance with the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Niśeśvarī Dakṣiṇāmnāya, in the venerable Parātantra. || 2 ||
The Third Chapter:
O Pārvatī, listen to the summary concerning the western side of the lion-throne, which was brought down by the illustrious Lord through many hundreds of thousands [of verses]. 1.
And the *Yāmala*, containing a hundred thousand verses, which is the various secrets of mantra,
[was produced], O Goddess, from the churning of your own navel by your own tongue in the past.
From her womb, the cosmic egg was born through that divine birth-canal;
from that time forth, O Maheśānī, she became renowned as the goddess Kujādevī.
Kubjikā, worshipped by the world, is distinguished by her aspects as the Elder and the Child;
she is the deity of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), proclaimed from the mouth of Sadyojāta.
Kubjikā is the primordial source of the worlds, whose form is the great dissolution;
she is the eternal teacher of the infinite, who has attained union with Śiva.
Flowing through many paths by means of the distinction between the eldest and the child,
Kubjikā, endowed with thirty-two divisions, rests upon Bhairava.
The god was seated upon a bull, resplendent with a complexion and form the color of the sky;
he had one face, three eyes, and bore eighteen arms.
In his right [hands], he holds a hand-drum (ḍamaru), an axe, an arrow, a sword, a goad, and a vajra; and a conch, a flute, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (8)
In the left hands, he holds a khaṭvāṅga, a trident, a bow, a shield, and a noose;
as well as a bell, a skull-cup, a flute, and the gesture of fearlessness that destroys all fear.
Her knees and left thigh are bound with a cloth, and she is hump-backed;
she has one face and three eyes, and her complexion is described as being like the dawn.
The goddess has two arms, bestows boons, stands upon a lion, grants fearlessness, her limbs are adorned with serpent ornaments, and her head is crowned by a crescent moon. 11.
Bound by the noose of the Lord of All Worlds, she possessed beautiful, full, and firm breasts;
she was resplendent with all ornaments and beautifully adorned with the primary marks. || 12 ||
Thus one should meditate upon Kujāmātā, the Bhairavī of the Western Tradition;
therein indeed exists Kubjikā, who follows the path of the Kula, in many diverse forms. (13)
It was divided by Siddhinātha and brought down by Śrīnātha;
it was revealed as the Kujāmnāya by the hero Kujeśanātha.
Navātmā, Śrīśikhānātha, Svacchanda, Śrīlaliteśvara, Krameśī, Trikhaṇḍā, Mahattārī, and Trikhaṇḍikā. || 15 ||
Triśuddhi, Ugracaṇḍā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍakapālikā, Annapūrṇā, Kapālī, Jvālāmālinī, and Kāminī. || 16 ||
The groups of Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, and the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga;
namely, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī. (17)
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā are remembered as the seventh;
Mahālakṣmī is the eighth. These are worshipped everywhere. || 18 ||
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodheśa, Unmattaka, Kapāla, the one named Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra is the eighth.
The Mātṛkā together with Bhairavī is indeed to be worshipped according to the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya); likewise, Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and the hosts of Yoginīs are remembered [as such]. 20.
Surrounded by a host of ḍākinīs, bhūtas, vetālas, and female servants, the six yoginīs are proclaimed as those who possess the great roars of the ḍākinīs and others. || 21 ||
The Ḍākinīs are proclaimed as sevenfold: Rākinī, Ghorā, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, Hākinī, and Yākinī. (22)
The deities are established and are to be worshipped; Bhairava is in the form of Ruru;
Sadyojāta is accomplished, as is that Kubjikā, the mistress of the wheel (cakranāyikā). 23.
The science accomplished by Aṅgiras was imparted to Dakṣa;
from him it was given to Nahuṣa, and from him to the lineage of Candra.
They are celebrated as the family deities (kuladevī) of both earthly kings and gentle beings;
they are remembered as bestowing many supernatural powers (siddhi) and being efficacious in all rites. || 25 ||
The Vidyā propitiated by Durvāsas is supported by the Nirācāla-kalā;
she is eternally devoted to the Vāmamārga, while the Dakṣiṇā [path] is devoid of fruit. (26)
Through the fivefold *makāras*, she becomes the bestower of fruits according to the worshippers;
she is free from the conduct of purity and impurity, stainless, and without support. (27)
The goddess Kubjikā, the Mother of the Kula, bestows swift accomplishment through the practice of the great siddhis such as aṇimā; she grants both liberation and worldly enjoyment. (28)
The Goddess has been described in many ways before you in the Śrīmata and other traditions;
and Manthānabhairava exists within the twenty-four Mata systems.
Thus ends the third chapter, concerning Kubjikā of the Western Throne, in the venerable Parātantra. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter.
I shall proclaim before you the tradition (āmnāya) based on Vāmadeva;
it is the supreme Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), originating from the Kālī-kula.
Kālikā, the fierce leader, possesses millions upon millions of manifestations; she is the goddess who bestows the perfection of the command, empowered by the splendor of Viṣṇu.
Nārāyaṇī, Mahākālī, she who is intent on protecting the world, Kālī, Kālī, Mahākālī, and Caṇḍayogeśvarī—thus [she is known]. (3)
Whether standing or walking, by constantly remembering [the Lord], one is liberated from great fear;
for all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are governed by Time.
She who reckons that time is Kālī; therefore she is remembered as Kālikā.
She is the mistress of many circles of wheels, possessing manifold divisions and great movements.
Indeed, even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are unable [to describe it fully] regarding the goddess Kālikā;
nevertheless, listen to at least a mere fraction [of her power] according to the Kumārī-krama.
Mahākālī is blue in color, with three faces and nine eyes;
her right face is yellow, while the northern face is like fire.
Her eyes are adorned with circles, her body possesses eight limbs, and she is slender of form;
she has a mass of tawny matted hair standing upright, with the crescent moon serving as her crest-ornament.
(17) Adorned with twenty-seven severed heads and smeared with splashes of blood, she is richly endowed with bones, earrings, and bracelets; her crown is a garland of skulls.
The sound of her tinkling bells and anklets was like the supreme roar of a hero’s gong;
she was a jackal mounted upon a corpse, her mouth brimming with blood.
Indra and the others— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
are the five agents, possessing yellow, dark-blue, red, smoke-colored, and white lusters respectively.
They hold weapons such as the vajra, staff, spear, and khaṭvāṅga;
with the index finger placed in her mouth, she is three-eyed and stands upon Śiva.
The goddess sits in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), her breasts full and elevated;
in her left hand, O beautiful one, she holds a skull-cup filled with blood. 13.
She holds a trident with a corpse in her right hand, and likewise a discus, a goad, and a mallet in her [other] right hands. (14)
In her left [hands], she holds a noose, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and the hair of a corpse;
she is the mere light-form, established through the activity of the power of consciousness. 15.
One should worship the nine faces of the Great Goddess in this form, which transcends the state of nirvāṇa, transcends all existence, and is beyond the reach of the senses.
The Great Goddess Kālikā possesses many forms of manifestation; she is eternal, the bestower of the perfection of the Command, and the one who sets forth the path of the Kaulas. 17.
Viṣṇu, who had come from the lineage of Makākulālikā, was overcome by you through your power;
the incomparable majesty of which cannot indeed be described. (18)
Durvāsas, Nārada, Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Kauśika—having been deficient by three, four, five, seven, and one [syllable] respectively, they attained perfection. (19)
The great siddhis beginning with *aṇimā* are known as her subsidiary accomplishments (*aṅgasiddhi*).
Kālī is the bestower of liberation and success; she is the sovereign mistress of nirvāṇa, the auspicious one (*śivā*).
Kaivalya is the sole accomplishment that illuminates supreme knowledge; the practitioner becomes Bhairava himself, directly free from old age and death. (21)
That prosperity which arises for the practitioner alone—rare even in the three worlds—is not produced for either the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) or for Śakra. || 22 ||
O Goddess, the sequence of the five faces is taught by the Five Kālīs;
she is the great goddess Guhyakālī, who is Vaiṣṇavī and possesses the form of Brahmā. (23)
All the millions of Mahābhairavas reside in Vāmadeva;
likewise, there are hundreds of thousands of billions of Gaṇeśas, Vaṭus, and Yoginīs.
Bhūtas, vetālas, ḍākinīs, servants, rākṣasas, birds, foam-eaters, crows, vultures, owls, garuḍas, and water-birds; || 25 ||
The Śṛṅgālī, Kaṅkatī, Yugā, and others of various forms and great strength—
those who know the sacred tradition (Āmnāya) declare here that the answer is beyond answering.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Guhyakālī, belonging to the Uttarāmnāya, in the venerable Parātantra. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter.
I shall describe the Upper Siṃhāsana, which indicates sovereignty over the three worlds;
it is the eternal Mistress of all Cakras, worshipped by all the Āmnāyas.
Consisting of all lion-thrones and seated upon the throne of Īśāna,
she is remembered as the Goddess Nārāyaṇī, the Māyā who is the Sovereign Lady of the Supreme Brahman.
Sleep, intellect, forgiveness, patience, hunger, modesty, memory, fortitude, wisdom, tranquility, splendor, and light—these reside in the nails of her toes. (3)
By the mere sight of her, one becomes the Lord of Lakṣmī himself;
her service, her amorous dalliance, and her path are all to be followed.
Having become equal to the king of kings, or even equal to the king of the gods,
and having enjoyed vast pleasures, one shall attain nirvāṇa in the end.
Sometimes becoming a woman and sometimes a man,
he shall destroy all the wicked ones in the form of Viṣṇu.
Pervading the world, that Māyā deludes both gods and demons;
having assumed a form of exquisite beauty, she is called Anūpā—this I shall tell you.
Resembling a ruby and appearing like saffron-water, she has beautiful eyebrows and lovely eyes; she is beautiful with a charming smile. (8)
She has a slender waist and four arms, her crest-jewel fashioned from a crescent moon;
she is three-eyed, her limbs adorned with every ornament, beautifully attired, and enchanting. (9)
She holds a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and five arrows;
she bears Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśa as her sandals upon the fifth pavilion.
The Supreme Goddess, seated upon the couch known as Sadāśiva, is celebrated as Parāśakti, Sundarī, and Tripureśī. (11)
The Goddess is the bestower of great liberation, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman;
she possesses many divisions, wide eyes, manifold forms, and is self-luminous.
Kāmeśvarī is the power (śakti) of Rudra, descended from the Pūrṇa-pīṭha;
Vajreśī is the eternal Vaiṣṇavī residing in Kāmarūpa. || 13 ||
Śaktīśvarī and Bhageśī are established at Jālandhara;
she is the power of Brahman, whose form is the wheel of the seat of intense radiance.
Dwelling in the sacred seat of Uḍḍiyāna, Śivā is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman;
she is the sovereign of all cakras, the mistress of all pīṭhas, and her very form is mantra.
She is the sovereign of all mantras, the queen of all gods, possessing a divine form;
she is the eternal mistress of the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya), free from parts, and without possessions.
The eternal Nityā of the sixteenfold Vidyā is established within the nine wheels; the eternal Mistress of the Nine Wheels (Navacakreśvarī) stands at the forefront of the nine corners.
The wheel that deludes the three worlds, which fulfills all desires;
the wheel that agitates all, which bestows all good fortune. || 18 ||
The supreme wheel that accomplishes all aims, which provides all protection;
the wheel that grants all desires, which bestows all spiritual attainments. (19)
The ninth wheel consists of all-bliss; its presiding goddess is dissolved within the universal bindu—this is proclaimed as the Śrīcakra.
Tripurā, Tripureśī, Sundarī, Puravāsinī, Śrī, Mālinī, Siddhāmbā, and Mahātripurasundarī [Mahātripurabhairavī]. || 21 ||
The multitude of many deities is dissolved within the wheels (cakras) and established there;
they reside in the bindu, in the triangle, in the intermediate space, and in the eight-cornered [lotus].
In the twelve-spoked [wheel], in the eight-petaled [lotus], and on all sides in the serpent-leaves;
in that which is numbered as sixteen petals, the square desires the qualities.
O Pārvatī, within that [mandala] which has four doors marked with lines, the three worlds are present;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, gemstone, or even on a leaf of birch bark.
O beloved, having seen [it] even on a ground-covering of silk, one who bows down has effectively bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices. (25)
He who, having fashioned a Śrīcakra, bestows it upon a practitioner shall become a giver of all things, a knower of all things, and manifestly equal to Maheśvara. || 26 ||
Indeed, he gave away the entire earth-circle, along with its mountains, forests, and groves;
he was truly a great devotee of Paśupati, and he was indeed the most excellent of Vaiṣṇavas. || 27 ||
He who gives all and sees all, who possesses knowledge of Brahman—he indeed is truly wise.
As for those great gifts (mahādāna) proclaimed by the sages who discourse on Brahman, [he has bestowed them all]. || 28 ||
One certainly obtains that fruit through the power of the Śrīcakra, which is declared to be the fruit of installing ten million liṅgas. (29)
One certainly obtains that fruit from the worship of the Śrīcakra; one attains with certainty the fruit of ten million consecrations of Viṣṇu. (30)
Having engraved it upon gold, silver, copper, a gem, birch bark, or a cloth, whoever wears it on the head, the neck, or even the arm, [attains the highest state]. (31)
Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the killing of a Brahmin—one is liberated from all such evils by wearing the Śrīcakra. 32.
Sins committed both knowingly and unknowingly go to dissolution;
everything is swiftly consumed by fire through the wearing of the King of Wheels (cakrarāja). 33.
It cannot be beheld by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, beasts of prey, or brahmarākṣasas;
nor can it be seen by ḍākinīs or śākinīs. || 34 ||

Even if one is situated in the birth ascendant with extremely cruel planets, or even if they are in their transit or in the ascendant, everything shall become auspicious through the influence of the benefic planets. || 35 ||
The Supreme Goddess, ever present, removes untimely death;
when the Supreme is present, what can other deities do? (36)
If one should cast off their life-breaths while wearing the Śrīcakra— whether on a battlefield, in a forest, in a forbidden place, or even in a state of impurity— [they attain liberation].
Even after committing very many sins through greed for the lunar fast, he will surely attain absolute liberation (kaivalya) and shall not be subject to rebirth again. || 38 ||
The messengers of Yama flee upon seeing one who bears the Śrīcakra;
or liberation is attained through the knowledge of Brahman, or by one who casts off the body in Kāśī. (39)
Or even by the wearing of the Śrīcakra, these three are the causes of liberation;
for all the hosts of gods reside therein, and indeed all dharmas reside therein.

All rivers such as the Gaṅgā, all bodies of water such as Puṣkara, human beings who strive for the goals of life, and sacred fields, groves, forests, and so forth—[all these are contained within it]. (41)
The fruit of sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha) shall indeed be obtained in its entirety.
Sundarī is traditionally remembered as being of two kinds, according to the left-hand (vāma) and right-hand (dakṣiṇa) modes of sacrifice.
The beautiful one is said to be of two kinds: Vāma and Dakṣiṇa, along with Sānalā. The Vāma [path] undoubtedly brings about all desires in a short time. || 43 ||
Through the yoga of the right-hand conduct, it is considered supreme for monks;
through the yoga of other types of conduct, one may swiftly obtain the fruit of accomplishment. || 44 ||
Through the right-hand practices (dakṣiṇācāra) prescribed in the Vedas, the fruit is exclusively liberation (kaivalya);
for this very reason, O Great Goddess, you are the manifest embodiment of Brahman.
The Great Goddess of sixteen syllables is established in the form of the expressed;
she is the fourth, the Great Vidyā, who is the manifest embodiment of the waking state.
Even with thousands of mouths and hundreds of tongues, I am not at all able to fully describe the sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā. (47)
She is the very essence of the knowledge of Brahman, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Goddess of gods, a single recitation [of her name] is equal to ten million Rājasūya sacrifices.
The sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā is never to be revealed;
the sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā [is not attained] without the grace of the Guru. (49)
O Prajāpati, whoever has seen this is to be consumed by the hosts of Yoginīs;
having been obtained through the grace of the venerable Guru, it must never be revealed.
One should never recite [the mantra] without the grace of the Guru;
obtained through the mercy of the venerable Guru, it bestows all prosperity and good fortune. (51)

She is the one who possesses the beauty of nectar, who bestows skill in the art of the sound of her rapid movement, who is endowed with a portion of good fortune, and who grants proficiency in the arts. || 52 ||
It bestows the beauty of the three worlds, as well as the power to attract the three realms, absorption into the Supreme Brahman, and supreme fame. (53)
The sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Dear One, these Great Vidyās issue forth like sparks [from a fire]. (54)
She is directly composed of existence and consciousness, eternal, the bestower of knowledge and liberation;
she is the lore that grants great prosperity, manifest in the form of the Imperishable.
The sixteen-syllable Mahāvidyā was declared of old as the Śrīvidyā;
O beloved, it must be protected from thieves just as one protects treasures.
The sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā must be protected even at the cost of one's life;
it should not be given to just anyone, but should be bestowed only upon one who would give their own life in return.
The king’s gifts of sovereignty, which are more precious than even his own life, consist of gold, silver, and copper, categorized as superior, middling, and inferior. (58)
Copper is said to yield a hundred-thousandfold merit, silver becomes a ten-millionfold, and gold bestows infinite fruit; what more, then, can I tell you? (59)
That first Vidyā is Bālā; thereafter Vāgbhairavī is remembered;
then comes Saṃpatpradā Śrīpadā, and then Tripurabhairavī.
Bindumālinī, Cillekhā, Hṛllekhā, Śrīparākalā, Ṣaṭkūṭā, Navakūṭā, Lopāmudrā, and Trikūṭikā. || 61 ||
The fifth is the ignorance of the five beloved ones, the venerable Kāmarāja;
this sixteen-syllabled Great Vidyā is indeed the venerable, supreme, and transcendent.
The palace situated beyond that is proclaimed as Śāmbhava;
the great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhis), beginning with atomization (aṇimā), are declared to be obstacles.
Mahātripurasundarī, the goddess of the five lion-thrones,
is the supreme Vaiṣṇavī deity, who is manifest as the very nature of the waking state.
The Supreme Goddess Prakṛti is eternal and possesses all forms;
she is the very nature of all living beings and remains pervading everywhere. (65)
She is the power of Śiva; she has no age, and is neither male, nor female, nor neuter.
She is the essential nature of all living beings and has the form of the primordial Liṅga of the Self.
That which is the cause of the arising of all things is designated as the *yoni*; its nature is that of the lion-throne, as declared in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya*. (67)
O Great Goddess, she is the very embodiment of the waking state, even in her slightest measure.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, concerning the sequence of the Upper Tradition of Śrīvidyā, in the venerable Parātantra.
The Sixth Chapter.
Now listen, O Sāvalijinamātṛkā, to this Āmnāya which accomplishes all rites and bestows swift results in the Kali age. 1.
On the Buddhist path, she is free from fear, possesses unimpeded splendor like that of fire,
and is renowned as Vajrayoginī, whose essence is the innermost self.
She has three faces and is red in color; her feet are in a dancing posture and she sits upon a corpse.
She has three eyes, wears a garland of rice, and is adorned with ornaments. || 3 ||
Her body is adorned with a garland of severed heads, she wears a serpent as a sacred thread,
is clothed in a tiger skin, and has a lion skin as her upper garment.
Vairocanī, preceded by Vajra, holds a vajra-bell and a boon-granting vessel;
she has four arms, stands upon a corpse, and has shaggy hair reaching down to her shoulders.
Holding in her hands a skull-bowl, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a ḍamaru drum,
she follows the Sugata and directly bestows swift fruit in the Kali age.
All these [traditions], following the Sugata and relying on various divisions, yield results only in this very life, are eternal, but do not bestow the fruit of final liberation. (7)
Kālacakra, Samvara, the one called Hayagrīva, Bhairava, Yogāmbara, and Kāleśa— these are all dependent upon Bali and Saugama.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, concerning the sequence of the lower tradition (*adhāmnāya*), within the division of the six traditions (*ṣaḍāmnāyabheda*) in the venerable *Parātantra*. 6.
The seventh chapter.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O omniscient Supreme Lord!
I consider that which arises from the Kālīkrama-kula to be most wonderful. || 1 ||
The mind trembles and a great horripilation arises;
how is that Goddess Kālikā divided into a hundred crores of forms?
O Supreme Lord, these three divisions have never been heard of anywhere;
rather, the mind shines forth when it abides by resorting entirely to the Kālikrama.

Who is the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī) and what is the division of the wheels? Who is she who is the supreme authority over all? O Lord, how is the division of the sequence (krama), the emergence of the family (kula), and the sequence of worship?
O Lord of Gods, what great fruit does one obtain through its worship? O Supreme Lord, what does the practitioner enjoy both in this world and in the next? (5)
How is it that Kālī is indeed without support, or how is she the devourer of Time? For you have declared her to be devoid of qualities, partless, eternal, and without divisions.
O Śaṅkara, tell me of the principal path followed by the Goddess, the Leader, if it is impossible [to describe] her face with its millions and hundreds of thousands of divisions.
In whose worship the entire [pantheon] becomes worshipped by Kālikā—
she is the one and only Supreme Eternal Goddess, whose form is consciousness.

(28) She who possesses all forms, the sovereign of all, whose nature is consciousness, the supreme one who is resorted to; in whom the universe arises, in whom it remains, and into whom it dissolves again—speak, O God, Great Lord! Salutations to you, O Moon-crested One!
Among them, who is the eternal mistress of the wheel (Cakreśvarī), what is her form, and how many are they?
Just as the deities are satisfied by the drinking of nectar itself,
so too am I fully satisfied upon hearing of the heroine and the sequence of her stages.
Speak, O Lord; you have no weariness, for you are omniscient, all-knowing, and present at all times.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said: "Salutations to Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, whose tongue is the devourer of Time, by whom millions of cosmic eggs are reduced to ashes."
Salutations to her who delights in devouring time, the Attractor of Time (Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī), for whose sport the entire universe serves as a ball.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you have asked:
the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) is indeed one alone, yet she manifests in many diverse forms. (15)
That goddess is eternal and partless, the illuminator of Brahman and Truth;
even with thousands of millions of faces and hundreds of millions of tongues, [she cannot be fully described].
O beautiful one, O Supreme Goddess, even with five tongues in five mouths, one cannot describe [her] even in a hundred years.
Among the hundreds of thousands of millions of divisions, I shall tell you just the tenth:
Kālikā, who is the most excellent among the divisions of the Krama and the bestower of liberation.
I shall explain those to you, the determination of the fivefold sequence:
she who consists of the Supreme Brahman, eternal, and manifest in the form of the waking state. (19)
Untainted, devoid of qualities, and eternal, she sports with the world through its qualities;
she is not manifestly male, nor female, nor neuter, nor is she material.
Of unmanifest form, supreme, and adorned with the qualities of the waking state, she is esteemed as the five elements: earth, air, water, fire, and space. (21)
For the sake of creation, she brings forth this form through her qualities;
she is the supreme goddess Dhāraṇī, extending from the earth up to Śiva.
Because of its vastness, it was called "Pṛthivī" (the Broad); from that, everything became great.
Sustaining all living beings, it is capable of being traversed everywhere. || 23 ||
The vital breath (prāṇa), endowed with the qualities of wind, returns equally everywhere;
by means of it, the fourfold world of living beings, both stationary and moving, exists.
That which is produced from water destroys everything with its qualities; that fire arising from water burns the entire world, whether it be the center or the very middle itself.
Blazing indeed with splendor, Splendor (Tejā) is supported by Him, because of His pervasiveness, His greatness, His partlessness, and His being the substratum of qualities. || 26 ||
For all the qualities of the Goddess are supported by space;
she is the mother of great good fortune and the bestower of great eloquence.
Possessing great beauty and auspiciousness, she is the destroyer of great death;
she is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods, and she removes the flood of sins.
The Goddess consists of all sacred fords; she is auspicious and consists of all dharmas;
she is meritorious and consists of all holy fields; she accomplishes the purpose of every undertaking. (29)
Bestowing great enjoyments, peaceful, and granting the fruit of great liberation, by her power alone, O Goddess, everything becomes pure; it cannot be otherwise. (30)

Whether one delights in the left-hand practice (vāmācāra) or performs the right-hand practice (dakṣiṇācāra), whether one is without conduct or possesses conduct—for such a person, no sin exists and no merit is found. (31)
What is the use of deliberating on conduct if one is devoted to the worship of Kālī? If one has not been initiated by Kālī, what is the use of deliberating on conduct? (32)
All ritual action that is devoid of proper conduct is rendered possessed of conduct by that [practice];
here, the rule of eating according to one's own will is considered equal to fasting.
By chanting the syllable and word of Kālī, whatever [sins] one has committed perish; even millions of great sins (mahāpātaka) are destroyed as if in play. || 34 ||
All sins are consumed like a heap of cotton by fire;
O Śivā, listen with a focused mind as I describe the extraction of the Cakra. 35.
One should again draw a dot (bindu), a triangle, a five-pointed star, a nine-cornered figure,
as well as an eight-spoked wheel, an eight-petalled lotus, and figures with ten and twelve corners.
Having drawn the sixteenth petal, one should draw the enclosure of severed heads;
O Goddess, this is declared to consist of fifty-four [petals]. (37)
O Dear One, one should draw a garland of severed heads at the tip of the trident consisting of fifty-four [heads],
and in the eight directions, the eight cremation grounds that bestow all desires.
A blazing fire, water, a corpse, a jackal, an owl, a terrifying sound, a crow, a vetāla, a shrine (caitya), and a liṅga—these are the eight [sites] in the cremation grounds. (39)
Having drawn [the diagram] in the eight directions around the funeral pyre, which destroys great sins,
one should place it upon gold, silver, copper, or even a gemstone that has been engraved.
The wise person should grind together sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, nābhi, saffron, vermilion, and red sandalwood. 41.
One should smear the vessel with that [substance] and draw [the lines] with a golden stylus—
straight lines, beautifully drawn, lovely to behold, and captivating to the mind.
Whether in an image, or on a cloth, or on a sacrificial mound, or in a book, or in the heart;
or even in a sword, or in a trident, or in a great vessel, or in a woman. (43)
These nine should indeed be worshipped; they are devoted to the nine sources (navayoni) and are dear [to the Lord].
One should worship them during the day, while practicing celibacy, for the sake of auspiciousness.
At night, Kālikā, the ruler of the Kula, the primordial Prakṛti, the Mother herself, who purifies the worlds through her divine play, should be worshipped according to one's desire.
This great mantra, proclaimed by Bṛhadbṛhatīvatī, is even greater than Reṇu;
I shall now describe the form of that which is formless, she whose nature is unmanifest.
Indeed, without meditation, even a complete ritual worship is considered to be of no value;
therefore, O practitioner, for the sake of your accomplishment, I shall describe to you the yoga of meditation. 47.
The divine Grandfather, having been propitiated by me, made a request; being pleased, he indeed granted it to Brahmā for the creation of the worlds.
Brahmā also bestowed the lineage of the Kālika family upon Pulastya;
he gave it to Viśravas, and Viśravas gave it to Dhanada.
Then all the lords of Laṅkā, belonging to the various lineages following the chronological succession—
namely Daśāsya, Kumbhakarṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa, and Mahendrajit— [approached].
Hiraṇyakaśipu, Vāṇa, Bali, Jālandhara, as well as Ambarīṣa, Māndhātṛ, Nahuṣa, the Haihayas, and others; || 51 ||
The hosts of sages, beginning with Nārada; Durvāsas, the son of Gādhi; and the Siddhas, beginning with Virūpākṣa—rejoiced there at their own will and with delight.
By even a small fraction of her grace, victory over the three worlds shall be achieved;
thereafter, urged by Brahmā, he [Rāma] set out for the slaying of the Lord of Laṅkā.
Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha bestowed upon the descendant of Raghu the Hṛcchatākṣarī,
consisting of ninety verses, at the Sūryūtīra Tīrtha.
In the mantra of three hundred syllables, she indeed bestows sovereignty over the three worlds; ten syllables of the Goddess were previously concealed by me with great effort. (55)
O Goddess, if one should know the three-hundred-syllable mantra to be complete, that meritorious soul is Bhairava himself; of this there is no doubt. (56)
She is renowned as Mantramātā, the bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds;
she is the mother of all mantras and the nourisher of every mantra. (57)
The Mother of Mantras, who bestows everything, has been described in many ways;
she is Tyamgirā Mahākālī, the bestower of liberation and bliss. (58)
(33) There exists no knowledge like this within the interior of the world;
it bestows sovereignty, bestows wealth, bestows liberation, and grants absolute isolation. (59)
By him, Rāma, Rāvaṇa was struck down;
she is the primordial Kālī, the fivefold sequence, she who is one yet has become fivefold. (60)
Kālī, born from the Kula, was brought down before [him];
the three-faced Kālī, consisting of nine syllables, remained as Kumārī. (61)
The first is Sṛṣṭikālī, the second is Sthitikālikā,
and the third is the fierce Ugrā, who possesses a divine form.
The goddess Kālikā, who is inexpressible, is established in the fourth state;
Bhāṣākālī, however, is the fifth, abiding in the state of non-duality.
All those [energies], being of undivided form, reside within the body of Guhyakālī; likewise, they reside in her body, her feet, and in the various limbs and members of her physical frame.
The limbs of her body are curved; she devours the directions beginning with the east.
She is the Great Swallower of the five times, she who is one yet possesses diverse forms. (65)
The Self, which is the universal element and is proclaimed as Guhyakālī—I shall now describe the meditation upon her, which destroys the sins of those who hear it; listen! (66)
Now I shall describe the unsurpassed yoga of meditation upon the Great Goddess;
by the mere knowledge of this yoga, the practitioner shall become a possessor of siddhi. 67.
Dark as the petals of a blue lotus, fashioned from sapphire,
she arises from the circle of light that is the expansive splendor of the Goddess of Wisdom.
Mahākālī has ten faces, twenty-seven eyes, and fifty-one staff-like arms; she has a human countenance. (69)
The lamp, the upward-facing mouth, and Caṇḍayogeśvarī are considered to be the great mouth consisting of light,
which bestows the state of Nirvāṇa.
Below that is the lion-faced [face], white in color and brilliantly radiant;
and below that is the jackal-faced [face], black, which terrifies the three worlds. (71)
The face of the Lord of Monkeys on the left is red in color and exceedingly fierce; the boar-face on the right is smoke-colored and terrifying.
The left face has the mouth of Tārkṣya and is tawny-colored with prominent lips; the right face has the mouth of a crocodile and is proclaimed to be greenish in luster.
One should meditate on the elephant-faced [form] on the left, white in color and exceedingly majestic, and the horse-faced [form] on the right of Kālī, dark in color. (74)
She has all-encompassing fangs and is formidable; she is three-eyed and makes a terrifying roar.
With eyebrows knitted in a frown, she is fearsome, with a mouth like the face of Time (Kāla) and a most excellent countenance. 75.
Her mass of tawny hair rises upward, adorned with a crest of the half-moon;
she wears a garland of bees beginning with Śveta and is decorated with hour-glasses made of various jewels.
A garland of heads is proclaimed to consist of twenty-seven severed heads joined with drops of blood, together with vajras and flowers.
The jewel of consciousness (cid-ratna), the skull-bowl (kādyam), the sword, the noose, and the spear;
the khaṭvāṅga, the severed head, the bow, the discus, and the resonant bell. || 78 ||
Vālapreta, Śaila, Kaṅkāla, Nakula, as well as Sarpa, Kuṭṭanī, Vaṃśa, Ṣaḍamra, and again Ovikā. (79)
Holding a fire-vessel, a staff, and a *sruva*-ladle in her eight arms, she possesses eight heads and carries a cloth, a mallet, and a *ḍamaru* drum.
The index finger that fashions the pill of the jewel of consciousness, the staff of *kuśa* grass,
the jar filled with jewels, and the trident that destroys the wicked.
The five arrows of Paśupati are the Vāṇa, the one that has not yet reached the lotus-island (Padmadvipa), the Kunta, the Pāṇijāta, and likewise the Phaṇikā and the Tomara. || 82 ||
A garland of flowers, a drum, a vulture, a svastika, a vardhanī vessel, a water-pot, and a sacrificial ladle—these remove the fear of cattle-disease. (83)
She holds in her right hands a *nandyāvarta* shell, an earring, a beautifully adorned piece of flesh,
a citron fruit, and a needle.
Clad in a tiger skin with a black antelope skin as an upper garment,
she was enriched by the beauty of a network of tinkling bells and resounded with the sound of heroic bells.
Resounding with the tinkling of anklets and terrifying with gurgling noises, adorned with golden armlets and bracelets, they were beautified by massive bones. || 86 ||
A garland of severed heads hangs from the goddess’s neck down to her feet; likewise, she wears a garland made of red lotuses and a string of dried skulls reaching to her forehead.
The waist of the Goddess is adorned with a girdle and a belt;
her neck shines with a sacred thread, and she wears a yogic cloth as an upper garment.

Adorned with gentle head-ornaments and decorated by the kings of the *nāgas* and others, she possesses the beauty of red earrings on her ears and is seated upon the throne of the five times (*pañcakāla*). (89)
Above that is the seat of Śiva, which is blue and marked by a crescent moon above the nāda;
it possesses the flesh of highly precious jewels, is black in color, and has four arms.
He has one face and three eyes, is adorned with the ornaments of Bhairava,
holds a chisel and a skull-cup in his hands, and carries a hand-drum and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Thus, the Bhairava-pīṭha is the supreme seat of the Goddess;
beneath that are the five corpses, and below those are the five causal deities beginning with Brahmā.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— the causal deities— are yellow, dark-blue, red, smoke-colored, and white in luster, respectively.
They bear weapons such as the staff, discus, spear, trident, and khaṭvāṅga;
with their three eyes fixed upon Śiva’s hand, they brandish the threatening gesture.
Tawny-red, the cause and source of the three qualities (guṇas), terrifying,
with adamantine fangs and a touch like a claw, she is the supreme Śivā upon the back of a lotus.
From Śacīpati (Indra) as the beginning to Anta (Nirṛti), the colors of the directions correspond to their respective deities:
Indra is yellow with a thunderbolt, and Vahni (Agni) is red with a spear.
Yama is black, holding a staff; Nairṛti is smoke-colored, holding a sword; Varuṇa has a white face and holds a noose; Vāyu is dark-complexioned, holding a goad and a banner. (97)
Kuvera with a saffron-colored mace, and the white trident of Īśāna— this is proclaimed to be known as the seat for the Lord of the Eight Directions.
The Kṛtayuga is to be known as white; the Tretāyuga is remembered as yellow;
Dvāpara is the color of dawn-red; and Kali is remembered as dark blue-black. (99)
The Ṛgveda is white in color, the Yajurveda is like gold, the Sāmaveda is known as red, and the Atharvaveda is said to be black. (100)
The Upavedas and the castes are said to be the ninth seat;
the seat is proclaimed to have the tips of its flames like a thousand suns. || 101 ||
The Goddess stands upon a lotus, dancing and eternally manifest;
or else she sits comfortably, presiding over all the gods.
Resplendent as a thousand suns, difficult to look upon and hard to approach, she is the eternal refuge of all the gods—Mālinī, the auspiciousness of victory. 103.
One should contemplate her licking the tip of her tongue with the syllable *mukta-hūṃ*;
or one should remember her dancing, even while standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.
The steadfast one, consisting of all mantras, the eternal conqueror of all fortune—thus should one meditate upon Mahākālī, inseparable [from the deity] and in the full bloom of youth. 105.
The Supreme Goddess, the Mistress of the Wheel, stands in the midst of the sequence of speech.
Now hear, O Pārvatī, the specific distinctions of the divisions of Pañcakālī. 106.
Mahākālī has nine faces and twenty-seven eyes;
her upper face consists of light and bears the name Caṇḍayogeśvarī.
The *cidratnavaṭikā* is indeed the seal (*mudrā*) of the Goddess of the Root; and the *vaktraikaratna* seal belongs to the one devoid of the five times (*pañcakālikā*). 108.
The face, weapon, arm, garland, seats, steps, ornaments, and colors are as they are in the case of Śrī Guhyakālī. (109)
O Maheśvarī, creation, maintenance, and dissolution occur within the Unnameable;
she is identical in form to Bhāṣākālī, but hear now her specific distinction from them. 110.
I shall describe those specific [forms] in detail and in their proper order:
Maheśvarī has a fresh face and resembles a dark blue cloud. (111)
In the previously mentioned King of Meditations (Dhyānarāja), there is another Great Goddess equal [to her]:
the Goddess is seated in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), with full and elevated breasts. 112.
Displaying her left fang with the tip of her tongue, she is in the triple-bent posture;
her long eyes are rolling with intoxication, yet she is intent on the gaze of meditation.
She is indeed named Cidratnavatikā, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
a vajra rests upon the tip of her index finger, and her form possesses a radiance like fire. (114)
One should always meditate upon the Mistress of the Senses, who is joined with twelve rays, situated within the wheel of withdrawal (saṃhāracakra), as the fleshless Ambikā of the hollow cavity. 115.
The goddess stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, pressing her teeth against the back of her upper lip;
she repeatedly licks her trembling tongue and utters the roar of the syllable HŪṂ.
The granter of boons, she who is beyond destruction, the one with matted hair and a lion-like mane, she who is endowed with ten powers and is the cause of the dissolution of the universe. 117.
Standing in the middle of the sequence of stability, with a slightly smiling face,
the goddess Kharvā, who has a protruding belly, is seated in the royal posture.
p. 39) Having abandoned Brahmakaṅkālavallabhā, Ajakṛṣṇa [worships] Mahākālī, who is sixteen-fold in nature and established in the state of persistence (sthitisthā). || 119 ||
She stands in the center of the sequence of emanation, endowed with a loud laugh;
she is upright, a bestower of the pledge, charmingly graceful, and slender of form.
Having set aside the Brahma-lute and bearing the moon and the sun,
one should meditate upon her as situated in the midst of the five yonis for the sole purpose of creation.
Residing in the center of the Wheel of the Ineffable (Anākhyācakra), the Goddess Bhāsā is identical with the universe;
she is the Goddess who has issued from all Kālīs and is established in the sixteen-spoked wheel.
Wearing two anklets upon her arms which surpass the moon and sun in brilliance,
Kālī, who originated from Viṣṇu, illuminates the world with her light.
The young maiden Kālī is all that consists of the cycle of existence;
the goddess has three faces and eight arms, and she is adorned with a garland of skulls.
Let those of dark complexion drink the divine blood; [let them hold] the noose, the goad, the thunderbolt, the trident, the skull-topped staff, and likewise the mallet. 125.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, who holds the severed head of a dead child in her hand and a skull-cup filled with blood, she bestows the fruits of various enjoyments.
For this very reason, this fivefold division is the cause;
from that arise all forms born of the sequence of Kālikā.
One should worship daily according to the prescribed rules and must not allow any omission of the rite;
one should perform that very vow exactly as it was undertaken before the Guru.
The forms of the deity and the mantra are the Guru alone; of this there is no doubt.
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all. (129)
The Guru alone is always to be worshipped for the sake of pleasing Kālikā;
for one submerged in blinding darkness, the Guru alone is the supreme refuge. (130)
Even among thousands of paternal uncles and sons, and even among hundreds of mothers and fathers, he is called "the Guru" because of the weightiness [of respect] due to these [parents]. || 131 ||
The expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin has been fully described;
however, O Pārvatī, there is no expiation for those acts committed against one's guru.
One should not conceive a sense of duality between the guru and the deity;
rather, through the transformation of one's own self, one should worship the guru alone.
"When the Guru is pleased, the entire world is pleased"—this is the command of the Supreme Goddess.
O son, neither mother, nor father, nor protector, nor kinsman, nor friend, nor king [is a refuge]. (134)
O Goddess, one should never, under any circumstances, treat the Guru with anything less than the utmost reverence;
for it is by his grace that one comes to know the three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving.
For one by whom the Guru has not been satisfied, his ritual action shall be fruitless;
yet from whose mouth the supreme Goddess, consisting of sound, has issued forth.
One should not deceive the Guru, even by one's disciples or by one's own life-breaths when they have reached the throat;
for by that [deception], Bhairava becomes light toward the deity and the entire mantra. 137.
One should not allow even the slightest breach regarding the guru, the deity, or the mantra;
by such a breach, one goes to hell and is indeed destroyed along with one's very roots.
One should satisfy the guru with effort and even at the cost of one's own life through faith;
otherwise, one will meet the fate of Vetāla, who was like a lamp-flame. (139)
By him who has satisfied the Guru, the three worlds have been protected;
O beloved, there is nothing superior to this, for the Guru is exceedingly dear.
O Śivā, you are bodiless, consisting of color and form, and pervading the entire universe;
the rites of purification, such as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), are performed for the Guru just as they are for one's parents. 141.
Without having done so, one passes [this life] for more than six hundred years.
O Goddess, the father is the giver of the body, and the guru alone is the giver of knowledge. (142)
There is nothing more venerable than the Guru in this ocean of worldly suffering,
from whose mouth has issued forth the body consisting of the sacred syllables of Brahman.
There is no doubt that he will certainly rescue [beings] from the ocean-like hells;
oh, I shall now proclaim the essence that grants all desires and purposes. (144)
The single-syllable, the nine-syllable, and the sixteen-syllable Vāruṇī [mantras], as well as the fifty-four-syllable and especially the hundred-syllable [mantra]. || 145 ||
The mantra of two hundred syllables, that of three hundred minus ten, and the thousand-syllabled one, O Goddess of gods—these are indeed the vital breaths of Kālikā. (146)
The extraction of the mantra consists of the sky, the supreme fire, water, and likewise the earth;
that science named Rāvaṇī, O beloved, bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
The single-syllabled supreme knowledge is remembered as the bestower of both enjoyment and liberation;
and here, O Pārvatī, there occurs the union of Śiva and Śakti. (148)
The goddess Mahākuṇḍalinī, worshipped by the great Rāvaṇi, [is] Vahni, Śiva, the syllable *n*, and Varuṇa. || 149 ||
Śikhī, Madhuhā, and Yuktā, along with Kālī, are declared to be Prāṇa;
having written Khphreṃ Mātmikā, one should write Mahācaṇḍaman.
Having bestowed the station of Yogeśvarī, this is that nine-syllabled Vidyā;
now hear that sixteen-syllabled Vidyā which is the very life-force. || 151 ||
By the mere instruction of which one becomes fit for the state of Brahman;
having extracted the three words, one should then write the "Great Roar" (mahārāva). 152.
O Goddess worshipped by the thirty gods, it should be known that [this state] is joined with the Night and the Spring;
when mounted upon Truth, it is eternal and swallowed by Contentment. 153.
Mounted upon the intellect of truth, she is swallowed by the subtle Lord;
from that arises the wheel, together with the digestive fire and Nārāyaṇa. (154)
Joined with Mādhava, O younger brother of Vala, one should write it again;
then Māyā, Caṇḍī, Kūrca, Rakṣā, and Mahārāva—one should write these again. (155)
O Goddess, one should apply the *nati* (obeisance) and recite the *śiras-mantra*;
this is declared as the King of Mantras, said to consist of sixteen syllables. (156)
Having offered five lumps before [the deity], one becomes the Moon of Great Sound;
this is declared to be the beginningless Great Mantra, the King of Syllables. (157)
The hundred-syllable king of mantras, as well as the five-hundred-syllable one;
the five-syllable primordial mantra, and likewise the eight-syllable mantra. || 158 ||
The Vidyā consisting of three hundred minus ten is declared to be the Mahāmantra;
that of two hundred and ninety is the Mahādevī, O lady of excellent luster. (159)
O Goddess, for the sake of attaining Śiva’s favor, this garland of a thousand syllables is indeed the rite superior to all others within the sequence of the Kula tradition. 160.
She is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, consisting of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā;
she dwells in the midst of the entire ocean and has the form of the entire ocean.
If this [teaching] obtained through the grace of the glorious Guru and transmitted through the lineage of the tradition is attained by good fortune, who else on earth could be more blessed? (162)
She is concealed within a human body, including her head; of this there is no doubt.
I am simply unable to describe the lineage of Kālikā. (163)
This sixteen-syllable Vidyā is remembered as the bestower of sovereignty and the giver of life;
she is the peaceful Kālī, the bestower of great bliss and the giver of breath. (164)

Vaikharī, being incapable of describing its qualities because it is dependent on other [sounds], is the very nature of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) and bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. 165.
O Goddess of gods, by a single utterance, ten million Vājapeya sacrifices, thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices, and likewise the Prādanya and Bhuvana sacrifices are attained. 166.
The merit born from bathing at Prayāga when the sun is situated in Capricorn is said to be increased a hundredfold if one performs the rite according to the Kālikā procedure.

Whatever merit is obtained by sequentially practicing the duties of the four stages of life (āśramas), and whatever merit belongs to the duty of one's social class (varṇadharma)—that merit is attained from the worship of Kālikā. (168)

O Goddess of gods, a pilgrimage to the sacred sites beginning with Kāśī, accompanied by three and a half crores [of other sites], is equal to this; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (169)

O Goddess of the gods, what more need be said? By reciting [this] one hundred thousand times, who would not become a possessor of supernatural powers (siddhi), through whose power the fourteen worlds belong to the Goddess? 170.
O Supreme Goddess, she existed for them in the form of their cause;
for whoever performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), the Vidyā became the limb that yields its fruit.
But without performing the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), a mantra will not yield its fruit;
[this mantra] is the mother of ten million cosmic eggs and the bestower of great liberation.
The great mantra issues forth like beloved sparks;
many divisions have been revealed from the presence of the Vidyā at its forefront. (173)
Everything has arisen from the Praṇava, and she consists of the Supreme Brahman; she is the remover of Māyā and its protector, and there is no other, O Mistress of the World. (174)
Through her illusory power (māyā), she deludes the entire world by assuming various forms and various names, while increasing [the lineage of] sons and grandsons. || 175 ||
She is eternally bound within the *Kāmasūtra* as both female and male;
she is all-pervading and dwells in the abode of Brahman. (176)
(45) This [mudrā], which binds good fortune and is proclaimed as the source of the universe, is established in the fourfold Vedic knowledge and brings the three worlds under control. || 177 ||
She is the Goddess whose very nature is direct consciousness, the bestower of objects of enjoyment;
she is the eternal giver of great prosperity, manifest in the form of the Imperishable. || 178 ||
Pervading the universe in the form of sixteen syllables, the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) exists as the nine-syllabled mantra, as well as the five-syllabled and the eight-syllabled mantras. || 179 ||
The single-syllable, the ten-syllabled, the hundred-syllabled, and the thousand-syllabled—pervading these classes of mantras, she remains established throughout the universe. (180)

That which is the essence among the four Vedas, that which is remembered in their auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), and that which is the greatest essence within the Purāṇas and the compendiums of law (smṛtisāras)—[that is this]. (181)

That is the most excellent essence, superior to all, the highest among the essences; just as butter is the essence extracted from curds, so is clarified butter the essence extracted from that [butter]. || 182 ||
Thus, that which is called Amṛta is the sustainer of the life-force of the gods;
likewise, it is so according to the command in all the scriptures, Vedas, and Tantras. (183)
Having extracted it from all essences, it was imparted to Brahmā;
from Brahmā it went to Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha to the descendant of Raghu.
It was given by him to the Universal Soul; thereafter, having established the various systems beginning with Advaita, it was brought down to the mortal world by the sage whose vision is knowledge.
By means of the vision of the three hundred-syllable [mantra], the power of the mantra was revealed;
by this, the goddess named Pratyāṅgirā brings about gentle accomplishment. 186.
(46) With the approval of Nārada, the goddess’s consciousness was divided in two;
it must be guarded with great effort, like a treasure from thieves. (187)
It should not be given to just anyone; it should be given to one who has bestowed life, who is stainless, who is tranquil, and who is dearer even than one's own life.
O Maheśvarī, this essence should be given to one who is established in knowledge.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Sūtra on the Determination of the Kālika-krama, in the twelve-thousand-verse [work] belonging to the sequence of the Supreme Tantra, the Karavīra-yoga within the Śrīmahāśrotaśiraścheda. 7.
The Eighth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
Salutations to the God of gods, the omniscient, the Great Soul.
Salutations to You, the creator, sustainer, and destroyer, who pervades all. || 1 ||
Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World! O Master, my mind has become restless with a desire to ask something; yet, out of fear, I am unable to speak.
Be gracious, O Supreme Lord; you ought to sever my doubt.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
"O Queen of the Gods, do not entertain doubt; there is no one dearer to me than you.
O Goddess, free from hesitation, ask by your own will whatever is desired in your heart."
O Goddess, whatever doubt you have, ask it according to your desire.
The Śrī Devī said:
Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, O Maheśvara!
When you became the Supreme Goddess Kālikā, whose form is consciousness (cidrūpiṇī).
O King, why did he go to the two [realms] with the approval of Nārada—he who was a knower of all scriptures, a hero, and the best of sages among practitioners? (7)
What kind of division indeed did Nārada formerly create between Śiva and Ṣaṇmukha?
The illustrious Sadāśiva said: "Blessed are you, you have accomplished your purpose; you know how to listen according to the truth.
Your mind is intent on hearing again these subtle distinctions. (9)
Supreme intelligence has been born; salutations to you, O Supreme Goddess!
You are the seventeen-syllable mantra, the supreme power of all knowledge.
The shatterer of Khaṇḍa, who shatters the egg of the fragments of fragments;
Kālī, situated within the wheel of fragments, is the seventeen-syllable Vidyā.
The letter *ka* in the form of a hooded serpent has *akula* as its bindu;
Lakṣmī, consumed by the drop and impelled by the three streams, is known as the seventeenth Vidyā. (12)
Abiding in the midst of the non-family (akula) and the family (kula), she is the digit (kalā) residing in the digits; she is the digitless digit.
Digitless and supreme bliss, she is the seventeen-syllable Siddhi.
The letter *ra* situated at the beginning, the letter *ra* situated in the middle, and those joined with the sound *ra* and the sound *ra*;
this is to be known as the great seventeen-syllable mantra, *rāvalīrāvalā*. (14)
Born from the desire for the beautiful and so forth, it is the great, surging utterance of *hūṃ*;
pervaded by the digits of the sound *rā* and *rala*, these are the seventeenth digit. 15.

Through the union of the perishable and the imperishable, she who abides by means of the word *Kālī* is the seventeen-syllabled Vidyā; there is no state of the Mistress of Yoga [attained] otherwise. 16.
Hahahāhahalalīnī, vilīnī, hahane, hasā;
līnā with the syllables hānā, dānā, and padaiḥ—this is the seventeen-syllable Vidyā. || 17 ||
Thus, the Supreme Goddess described the seventeenth letter, which is the intense, all-pervading state of the Krama, devoid of qualities, the Supreme Sovereign. (18)
Two hundred and ninety syllables are proclaimed by their color;
the Vidyā, when deprived of the triple qualities, is celebrated as being divided into three parts. (19)
There is no distinction here among the nine and sixteen syllables;
by means of this vidyā, O Goddess, one abandons birth and death.
The best of sages, such as Nārada and others, and the yogis, such as Kapila and others,
having become conquerors of the three worlds, indeed wander about according to their own will.
O Goddess, with unimpeded movement and having attained the knowledge of the three times, he who is the Lord of Existence (Bhavasvāmī) [saw] a deer in the form of a hand in the city named Śoṇita.
The lord of sages, Nārada, bestowed it upon Kṛṣṇa; among those [powers], Hari employed the power of enchantment (ālambhana) to delude Hara.
In the past, Vāsudeva also gave it to Pārtha for his protection,
so that it might become as fit for Śiva as the moon-like flower once enjoyed by Bhṛgu.
In the same way, although the syllable-less reality is joined with syllables, the Goddess herself, the supreme Mistress of Letters (Varṇeśvarī), does not cause it to be extracted through writing. 25.
Surely a curse occurs and the loss of the mantra arises;
Kālī becomes averse [to him], and he becomes a refuge for the sinful. (26)
O Goddess of gods, always place [it] in the heart from ear to ear;
having emerged from the mouth of the Guru, it remains in the heart by way of the ears. (27)
Just as writing in water [vanishes], so too should be the extraction of the mantra;
one must never write the Vidyā—which bestows both enjoyment and liberation—in a book.
Having understood the auspicious and inauspicious karma resulting from a residence of one year, the mantra should then be imparted, if one desires one's own welfare. (29)
But he who bestows a mantra upon an unexamined disciple will dwell for a very long time in a most dreadful hell. (30)
Therefore, with every effort, this should never be disclosed;
the Goddess is pleased with him who possesses a faithful intellect. || 31 ||
Whatever doubt arises, those [doubts] are vessels of suffering;
through doubt there is loss of accomplishment, so one should take refuge in the non-conceptual.
One should not deliberate there over what ought to be done and what ought not to be done,
even by me, nor by Viṣṇu, nor by Brahmā, nor by the sages together.
Taking up a single vessel, she remained free from conceptual construction as she supported the gods, gandharvas, daityas, and others—rakshasas, pannagas, and humans. (34)

Since these [limbs] are drenched with the seven bodily fluids and bring forth the outflow of impurities and urine, what is the use of reflecting upon them? One should practice the state free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). || 35 ||
When the sun has risen, can darkness remain in the worlds? Likewise, by the power of the Goddess, who would deliberate upon worldly conduct? (36)
O Goddess of gods, what is the use of speaking at length? It must be guarded with great effort;
O Great Sovereign, for the sake of all accomplishments, it must be guarded with great effort. (37)
If one practices openly, one meets with death and the loss of spiritual accomplishment occurs;
for whatever conduct is prescribed in a particular mantra, such is the dharma therein. (38)
One who has accomplished his purpose would not be born again, whether in heaven or even in liberation;
neither unrighteousness nor sin and the like arise for him, nor does he experience rebirth. (39)
Moreover, whether it be a great dharma or a mass of merit, it increases;
for whatever has arisen in the entire world, [it is accomplished] through one's capacity. (40)
Therefore, O Brahmin of noble vows, one who knows all the Vedas should understand that whether pure or impure, everything has the nature of Śakti-Brahman, according to right conduct.
Even in the state of a caṇḍāla or in the highest evil, the Self is indeed perceived everywhere.
Know that the Self is Brahman; one should abandon deluded cognition. (42)
Knowledge alone is the supreme reality; therefore, take refuge in knowledge.
By means of the path of knowledge, one should completely abandon all conceptual construction.
One who possesses conceptual thought certainly becomes a partaker of great faults and sin;
from the union of Śiva and Śakti, the body is produced, consisting of the vital energy (rajas) and semen (śukra). 44.
O Supreme Goddess, she who is merged in the Supreme Brahman is the supreme object of expression;
indeed, there are various types of substances such as clarified butter, honey, and liquor. (45)
O lady of excellent gait, in omniscience no fault of sacrifice is found;
how could there be the slaughter of a horse in the great Aśvamedha sacrifice? (46)
Water, milk, clarified butter, honey, maireya wine, sugarcane juice, the fruit of the pauṣya tree, grain produced from trees, and that which is prepared from buttermilk; || 47 ||
And even that which arises simultaneously, though it be of various and many kinds, if it is conditioned by ignorance, immediately becomes a creator of great sins. (48)

By the mere act of worship, one who knows the mantras becomes free from the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, and so forth, and attains the state beyond conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). (59)
"Bring all the water-dwelling creatures along with a jar full of water;
when placed for seven days, the water will be endowed with life. (50)
"O beloved, there is nothing whatsoever that is not food, such as all kinds of milk and so forth;
O beautiful one, the fire remains equal toward all trees. (51)
The supreme teachers must recognize consciousness within all beings;
through the friction of wood and other materials, the Goddess is made manifest and is called Brahman.
Just as that wood is consumed by that very fire, so too is this entire world, consisting of Brahman,
consumed in the hereafter through the total abandonment of both merit and demerit.
Or even that which is entirely free from female menses, O beloved—whatever exists, one should examine it as being one's own urine and so forth; for delusion alone is the cause. (54)
One should know that food is Brahman, for from it arises the existence of all beings;
