since it is the support of various living creatures, how can that excrement be considered defiled? || 55 ||
O Goddess, the consumption of cow urine and the eating of cow dung have been prescribed as penances for liberation from such acts as the killing of a Brahmin. (56)

O Supreme Goddess, there is no doubt that those who are deluded regarding excrement and urine commit a fault; by that very [delusion], O Sovereign Lady, the body is born from the menstrual flow of women.
By that which is conceptualized and purified, the supreme state is attained;
indeed, the seed of the Puruṣa is designated as "Vindu. (58)
O Supreme Goddess, this body is indeed the *bindu*, bearing the form of Śiva.
At that time, because of the nature of Śiva, there is truly no defilement by the *śāstra* and so forth. (59)
O beautiful one, by what means is the impurity of the body washed away?
O lovely lady, everything is purified by the path of knowledge for one who is free from conceptual construction.
O Great Goddess, a man who engages in conceptualization becomes a partaker of sin; he is undoubtedly like a mere infant within the womb of his mother. 61.
That which, due to its unchanging nature, cannot be disparaged by anyone else is free from fault; everything else would be associated with defect, even if it were entirely auspicious.
Knowledge consisting of the bliss of Brahman becomes identical with the Supreme Brahman;
having known that, O Supreme Goddess, O fair-faced one, I shall speak. (63)
O Supreme Goddess, there is no Brāhmaṇa who is not Brahman, nor a Kṣatriya who is not Kṣatra; there is no Vaiśya who is not Vaiśya, nor a Śūdra who is not Śūdra.
O Supreme Goddess, in the state of higher reflection (vicāra), neither Puṣka nor Eṣa is truly abundant;
know for certain, however, that the Supreme Self alone is so for all. 65.
Water fallen from the sky flows along a downward path;
all that has entered the midst of a village, such as excrement, urine, and the like, [flows out]. (66)
O Goddess of gods, when even all these—mixed with the blood of a dead cow, a snake, a cat, and a donkey—are united in the Gaṅgā; || 67 ||
That very [water] is the nectar of the Gaṅgā; turbidity does not remain at all.
Whatever defects exist in feces and urine are indeed caused by delusion alone. (68)
The menses of a woman is declared to be pure, since it has issued forth from the body;
by means of that which is primarily blood and other [elements], the supreme state is attained. (69)
The seed of the person is called the *bindu*; semen is the cause of all. Why, then, is that body censured? (70)
When a man emerges from the womb due to the contact of the vulva and the phallus at the time of birth, who then would not be a violator of his guru’s bed? (71)
Listen, O beloved, to this knowledge which is free from merit and sin:
I alone am the mother of ten million cosmic eggs, whose nature is the syllable *Aham*.
Having enjoyed the entire world through various means for the sake of sport,
[I perceive it] according to the division of the potter's wheel, just as the space within a jar [is distinct] in each jar.
O Supreme Goddess, it is seen that [the ether] exists pervading the sky;
one should conceive of a division within the pot as a division within the ether itself. (74)
Just as the individual soul residing in the body remains pervading everywhere upon the destruction of the body, O fair-faced one, therefore the state of Brahman is great.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, one should always remain free of conceptual construction;
thus, in that which consists of pure consciousness, there is knowledge of equality toward all living beings. (76)
And equality exists among all castes; there is no doubt about this.
Just as equality prevails through the light of the sun, so it is here. (77)
Furthermore, when given to another, it dispels darkness in an instant;
sandalwood dries up all urine and the like, yet it never dries up mud.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, one becomes identical with all things;
yet, O Beloved Goddess, it should be understood that accomplishment comes through the grace of the venerable Guru. (79)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Determination of the Ultimate Reality, in the venerable Parātantra. || 8 ||
The Ninth Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O God, Lord of the World, [tell me] how I may accomplish the ritual applications and so forth."
O Śaṅkara, tell me likewise how the practitioner [should proceed] through the distribution [of the offerings].
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which indicates complete perfection,
by means of which a hero may accomplish the lineage of the Vīrācāra tradition.
But he who desires to perform the ritual application without having first completed the preliminary service (puraścaryā) will become a vessel for tens of millions of great sins.
O Goddess, there is nothing higher than this: those who defile the path of the Kula.
Therefore, even at the cost of all one's possessions and even by the sacrifice of one's life, [one must always protect it]. || 4 ||
Through action, mind, and speech, one should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa);
the mantra-practitioner, having conquered his senses, should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya) while reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables.
During the day he should observe celibacy, and at night he may act as he desires;
having performed the preliminary rites of the five elements (pañcaka), he should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed ritual.
One should not perform it there deficient in its limbs or its retinue;
one should perform the oblation ten times the number [of mantras recited], using bilva leaves soaked in ghee.
For the sake of pleasing the Goddess, one should satisfy her with goat meat smeared with the three sweets;
indeed, one should gratify the Goddess with nectar using portions equal to one-tenth of the oblation.
(56) Sprinkling (mārjana) is declared to be one-tenth of the libation (tarpaṇa);
one should indeed perform the great feeding of virgins (kumārī-bhojana) as one-tenth of that. || 9 ||
In the Kali age, the practitioner should perform the *puraścaraṇa* four times over;
having received initiation, one must certainly not delay the *puraścaraṇa*.
Knowing the fickleness of life, one should contemplate one's own ultimate welfare;
for if one dies after receiving initiation without having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), [the result is lost]. 11.
One would surely become one with Brahman after a hundred years without support;
therefore, O Goddess, one should resort to *puraścaryā* with all one's soul. (12)
Or one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* during an eclipse of the moon or sun;
having performed the recitation from the moment of contact until liberation [from the eclipse], it is called *puraścaraṇa*.
One should perform all rites according to the ten-fold division as previously described;
now listen, for I shall presently explain the ritual applications (prayoga).

One who is unable to perform the Vīradīkṣā after first worshipping according to the rules—whether situated in a cremation ground, in the right-hand Śiva tradition, at home, or in a vehicle—[should proceed as follows]. (15)

He should constantly offer the three kinds of lamps and other offerings, especially on festival days; he should be endowed with truthful speech and fortitude, and be free from desire and anger. || 16 ||
Whether joined by his powers and assistants, or accompanied by heroes and helpers,
or even devoid of assistants and materials, he subsists on alms at the end of the night.
First, for the purpose of purifying the body, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand and one times;
then, once the Goddess is pleased, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) exactly as previously described by me. (18)

Then, the practitioner of mantras should perform one hundred thousand recitations during the day while abstaining from food; if he is unable to maintain the visualization after eating, he should eat only once at the time of twilight.

Having performed the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and recited the Gāyatrī mantra an even number of times, one should then perform the recitation at night according to one's ability and in the proper sequence. (20)
Thereafter, for the sake of attaining perfection in the mantra, one should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth [of the total recitation].
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, by performing the worship of a maiden, success will certainly be achieved.
Alternatively, one should perform the recitation twice as long for up to seven days;
in the case of malefic planets and the like, the pacification of the planets occurs at the end of the sprinkling and the fire-oblation on the eighth day.
At the three junctions of the day and at midnight, for one, two, three, or four days,
one is liberated from disease through a pacifying *homa* performed according to the specific direction of the wind and other elements.
Beginning on either the eighth or the fourteenth day, Hara [should perform] a hundred [recitations];
through the performance of a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number, a great pacification (mahāśānti) will clearly arise.
The mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra five hundred times; for whomsoever he desires, he should offer three hundred oblations.
At the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice (homa), he shall behold [the deity] from his own seat and shall attain prosperity. || 25 ||
Having offered three hundred oblations and recited [the mantra] on the eighth day,
and having recited it at the conclusion of the fire-offering while being consecrated by sprinkling, a person attains nourishment.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times, one should indeed offer five hundred oblations;
through the consecration (sekata), one attains the nourishment of the worlds of the Nāgas, Aśvas, Gās, and the eight [classes of] beings.
By turning the *nirgalādgalayantra* for oneself or for another at the three junctions of the day, one becomes submissive within twenty-one days. (28)
Having taken pebbles from a cremation ground, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
wherever Gaurī casts them, there shall be the bursting of thunderclaps.
Holding the staff of Bhūtāṅkuśa consecrated three times with mantras, one should loosen and release the fastenings of boats, carts, and mechanical devices.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times over sand, one may ward off the agitation caused by the threads of *dūrvā* grass, poison, and wicked beings within a miserable family. (31)

Having recited [the mantra] seven times over black mustard seeds, a person who is seized by spirits and the like should strike them on the heart while forming the mudrā; thus they will certainly be abandoned.
Having performed [the rites] for quartan fever and the others, and having recited [the mantra] seven times, they do not return;
even those difficult cases cease through the sprinkling [of water] and the incense of *guggulu*.
Likewise, various diseases such as scabies, boils, and carbuncles— O skillful one,
by reciting [the mantra] seven times, it destroys them through sprinkling, drinking, or bathing.
Water consecrated twenty-one times with this mantra will destroy poison, whether it be of a stationary or mobile nature, by its mere drinking. (35)
Flowers, food, *siddhārtha* seeds, and the ashes of a cremation ground—these seven mantras will slay an enemy and for the purpose of deluding that enemy. (36)
For one who is constantly devoted to worship, there shall be no loss of dice [or wealth] when placed upon a large vessel, a heap of grain, or jars filled with wine. (37)
Having written this on a leaf and placed it within a citron fruit in a treasury, one should recite the mantra;
wealth equal to that of Kubera shall never perish. (38)
In a stable for elephants, one should worship lotuses with offerings;
the elephants will never perish, and their prosperity will increase.
And having constructed a nine-compartment layout with groups of horse-positions,
those auspicious horses, being worshipped, do not perish but attain prosperity.

Having recited the mantra seven times over white guñjā seeds along with their stalks, as well as a piece of tiger-skin and a cowrie shell, one should wear them on the face; then no fear of weapons shall arise.
(59) If one wears on the neck a hundred thousand mantras written on the skin of a black cobra, they will increase in power, and one’s life and wisdom will become firm. 42.

On a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, a woman who has gathered ripe bilva fruits consecrated five hundred times with this mantra and bathes with that water shall give birth to a son, even if she was previously childless. (43)
A flower garland consecrated with exactly one hundred and eight [recitations] should be placed upon the neck of whomever; such a person shall be victorious in battle with anyone.
He who, having fasted for a day and night, recites [the mantra] while remaining free from anger—whether for his own sake or for the sake of another—his untimely death shall perish. (45)
One who possesses the Puṇḍarīka-aṃśu-nāva [mantra] shall see the secret [deity] face-to-face when it is radiant;
by reciting the syllables a thousand times, one sees the treasure of the ointment.
Taking earth from a crossroads and reciting [the mantra] twenty-five times over it, one should apply it to half of the house;
thus, sleep will be curtailed and the bond [of the husband] becomes difficult to break.
If one consecrates sesame seeds, rice, and white mustard seeds ten times each with the mantra, and then casts them together, the enemy shall not step upon that spot. (48)
If one should subtract the number of the lunar day from one hundred and twenty-five, wherever the remainder falls, there the person shall become ill. (49)
Wherever the practitioner throws rice, unbroken grains, white mustard seeds, and ashes consecrated with a hundred recitations of the mantra, there health prevails. (50)
If one stands in water reaching only to the neck and recites [the mantra] five hundred times,
and likewise performs a fire-oblation (homa) with Varuṇa, a great rain will certainly fall.
O Dear One, the practitioner of mantra should recite it fifty times and perform fifty oblations;
within seven days, he will bring even the Lord of Śacī under his control, of this there is no doubt.
Having recited the mantra five hundred times, the practitioner of mantra should then perform a fire-oblation (homa) of five hundred [times];
having again recited it five hundred times, he should likewise offer white mustard seeds and unbroken rice grains for the sake of accomplishment.
If it is worn on the head, the neck, or the arm, it brings about the immobilization of the one who plays [with dice].
Having offered a hundred oblations of Apāmārga, its ash is given to whomsoever [it is intended for].
It is true that he becomes unfortunate and shall suffer the destruction of his joy;
however, by combining three hundred [beads] of *siddhārtha* and *guggulu* together, [this is averted]. // 55 //
And at the conclusion of the oblation, great joy and the destruction of sorrow arise;
one should perform the oblation with eight hundred seeds of gold for seven days.
One quickly becomes insane, or [one may consume] vabhrūla mixed with ghee;
for seven days and nights, one should recite [the mantra] endowed with faith. (57)
During the day, one should practice celibacy, and at night one may act as desired;
one should offer five hundred oblations of cotton seeds, husks, and sesame oil combined.
O Goddess, on the twenty-first day, it may take away even the splendor of Śakra;
on the third lunar day of Jupiter or Venus, one should perform worship and recite the mantra a hundred times over a water-pot.
Having offered the three sweets (trimadhu) through sprinkling, one who has lost their fortune regains prosperity;
having formed the *viṣṭapna* mudrā, [extending] from the thumb to the top of the head. 60.
Having cut [the thread] five hundred times and offered oblations, he shall marry his own kinswoman;
[this is done with] vermilion joined with unbroken rice grains, consecrated one hundred and eight times.
Having prepared it and placed it in the hand of a maiden, one who is possessed should speak;
[the powder] made from the ash of *rājikā* smoke, consecrated ten times. (62)
The pacification of great diseases is certain by merely bathing with oil or ghee that has been consecrated eight times. (63)
By providing food, drink, and clothing, she brings forth easy childbirth;
having worshipped a jar at the head of the bed, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. (64)
In matters concerning one's welfare or harm, one should act by consulting with oneself and others;
having taken up a dark-colored garment, one should perform the recitation of Kṛṣṇa one hundred thousand times. 65.
In that very manner, remaining invisible, he plays skillfully upon the surface of the earth;
having placed twenty-five thousand barley grains in his hand, he should mutter the mantra.
At the conclusion of the recitation, the wise one should consume [the substance], and he shall become equal to Vāgīśvara.
When the hero performs half as many oblations of lac with Kadamba flowers, [he attains the same result].
"O Vetālas, arise quickly from the sacrificial pit; then success shall be achieved.
Kākinī is satisfied by the *vīra*-oblation, as are the bhūtas and piśācas. (68)
By performing a daily oblation of half of half a hundred thousand [offerings], one should give [the fruit] to another who desires it alone;
taking [the offering] within the hands of a maiden, one should perform half a hundred thousand [oblations] in the cremation ground.
Having recited [the mantra] over the lord of the past, future, and present worlds,
he took two human eyeballs that had been consecrated with a hundred mantras of lac.
Having applied a tilaka on the forehead with a well-blended mixture of saffron, agallochum, camphor, and gorocana, whoever should meditate [upon him] shall become submissive. (71)
Whoever applies a tilaka after consecrating it one hundred times with mantras shall be victorious in battle, in the royal court, in gambling, and in dispute.

Having placed white mustard seeds in the belly of a water-pot at dawn on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, and having worshipped it in the morning while mixing it with honey, one attains success. (73)
Having placed [it] in the mouth and recited [the mantra], one will achieve victory in debate.
The root of the *śivaśrapuṃkhikā* plant, consecrated by one hundred and eight recitations, [should be used]. (74)
O Goddess, for those who have bound themselves with head-cloths to ward off the arguments of opponents, there exists therein no distinction between right conduct and deviant conduct. (75)
Even though she was devoid of proper conduct, she became possessed of good conduct through the power of that goddess; what is the use of saying more? I shall state this essential point. (76)
Having made a seat of human skin, one should perform worship using a human skull-cup;
one should accomplish this with unwavering concentration, as instructed by the mouth of the Guru. (77)
Filled with a cause resembling lac-dye,
having bestowed the fruit therein, in the midst of that vessel filled with causes.
On the eighth or the fourteenth day, and especially on Śivarātri, one should perform worship at night, worshipping thoroughly.
Just as one performs the worship of the Śrīcakra, so indeed should one perform everything;
one should place the great vessel upon the triangle within the Binducakra.
In the fivefold Kālī, however, there are indeed five carukas on the five spokes in sequence; O auspicious one, there is nothing superior to this in the worship of the Kālikākrama.
An enjoyer shall certainly attain the happiness of heaven, liberation, and the perfection of command;
this is the truth, the truth, O Great Goddess—I speak this to you as it is. 82.
But he who acts otherwise, through fallacious reasoning and improper logic, will only undergo exhaustion and shall not attain perfection. (83)
Thus has this Kulakrama of Kālikā been fully explained to you—
the supreme, divine procedure derived from the scriptures of the Kālikrama.
It should be guarded with great effort and not given to just anyone;
for it belongs to one who is devoted to the Guru, as it consists of the Great Scripture. 85.
Having seen something delightful, such as flowers or fruits, or even clothing and ornaments—whatever is pleasing to oneself, auspicious, and rare upon this earth—(one should not take it). || 86 ||
Having first offered it to the Guru, one should bow and retain it within oneself;
one should cause it to be given to a worshiper who follows the lineage of the Guru’s tradition.
When the Guru is satisfied, the Kālikākrama is satisfied;
by whomsoever this scripture is written, and in whose hands it remains. 88.
Wherever one duly worships the Supreme Goddess while staying there,
he indeed lives for six months without any obstacles, and even throughout his entire life.
By whomsoever this book, the lineage-succession of Kālī, is worshipped in its entirety, by him Kālī, the destroyer of Time, has been worshipped. (90)
She always measures the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, with time;
and that very time, Goddess Kālikā herself, measures age after age.
There is no sacrifice equal to Kālī, no austerity equal to Kālī, no dharma equal to Kālī, and none like Kālī upon this earth. (92)
(64) He should be known as one liberated while living; he is indeed a great Pāśupata.
Know him to be a great yogin who has taken refuge in the path of Kālikā. 93.
I am the god Mṛtyuñjaya; he shall be the performer of auspicious rites.
Especially in the Kali age, Kālī must be worshipped with great effort.
O Dear One, he who knows the deity-joined obstacle and the place free from obstacles is the god Bhairava; such a one becomes equal to Rudra in his stream of realization. 95.
For the benefit of practitioners, he appears both as one and as many; thus, the currents of various tantras have come to possess diverse lineages. (96)
In that regard, regarding the distinctions, there are various names for the one power manifested in a thousand ways:
Maṅgalā, Mahāmāyā, Caṇḍakāpālinī, and Śivā. (97)
Cāmuṇḍā, Carcikā, Caṇḍā, she who brings about creation, maintenance, and destruction;
the Ineffable One, the Great Language, Guhyakālī, Jayā, and Parā. 98.
Siddhilakṣmī, Viśvalakṣmī, and Mahāpratyaṅgirā are remembered;
[so too are] Sundarī, Tripurā, Cāru, Ugracaṇḍā, and Prakāśinī. (99)
She has become divided in many ways and has resorted to various distinctions; though she is one, she is multiform—this one should know with divine vision. 100.
He alone is the most excellent practitioner, a vessel for the knowledge of accomplishment;
he alone is the most excellent practitioner, a vessel for the knowledge of accomplishment.
Devoted to practice, he will certainly partake in all accomplishments. 101.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Mahākaravīrayoga* within the *Śrī Śrotaśiraścheda*, a supreme tantra. 9.
